quote: Nobody says good job, nobody says wait for the others
why: reports nobody's reaction to the pace as proof the pace is normal, instead of showing one character's specific response
suggestion: The teacher hands Ruth the next page before Chloe has finished turning hers.

quote: Nobody says good job, nobody says wait for the others
why: stacks two parallel negative clauses back to back, the exact stacked-negatives pattern the guide says to restate as one positive statement
suggestion: They just keep handing out the next thing, all day, until the day is over.

rule_name: Hedge Where the Character Could Not Know, Cut Filler Everywhere Else
quote: they just keep handing out the next thing
why: "just" softens a claim the narrator is entitled to state plainly; it isn't hedging an estimate Chloe couldn't know
suggestion: they keep handing out the next thing, all day, until the day is over

quote: feels it in there
why: routes the sensation through the filter word "feels" instead of rendering the physical stimulus directly
suggestion: There is no part of it where she sits with a book in her desk, its corner against her palm.

quote: She's slow at writing, she has always been slow at writing.
why: restates the same claim twice in one breath with almost no new information, telling the reader the first clause wasn't trusted to land
suggestion: She's always been slow at writing.

quote: knew it while it was happening
why: routes Chloe's self-awareness through the filter verb "knew" instead of rendering what told her she was bad at it
suggestion: she was bad at that, and the timer kept ticking while the man watched

quote: there's nothing in them she'd take out
why: "nothing" is the exact vague placeholder the rule names, standing in for a specific judgment about her own sentences
suggestion: she reads them back twice and leaves every word where it is

quote: puts the pen down without any fuss about it
why: defines Kavi's manner by what it is not (no fuss) instead of stating positively how he set the pen down
suggestion: sets the pen down flat, evenly

quote: He isn't bothered about any of it
why: defines Sam's reaction by absence instead of naming what he actually does or feels
suggestion: Sam shrugs and checks his own page instead.

rule_name: Banned Constructions, Assert Nothing, Show the Substance
quote: Six would have been the best one in Mrs. Aldana's room.
why: a bare ranking verdict in narration ("the best") that hands the reader a conclusion instead of the fact that would let them reach it
suggestion: Six would have been the longest one read aloud in Mrs. Aldana's room.

rule_name: Dialogue Attributed to Furniture, Not People
quote: to nobody, to the room
why: attributes Ruth's line to no listener at all in a room full of people, the furniture-avoidance device the rule says stops registering once overused
suggestion: "I told you," Ruth says, not looking at anyone in particular.

quote: and that nothing on their bridge was holding any of the corners at an angle, and that this was true of every corner they built
why: three "that" clauses of unequal weight are strung together with flat "and...and" coordination instead of subordination
suggestion: it was a corner, because nothing on their bridge was holding a corner at an angle, not one of them

rule_name: Crutch Phrases That Have Stopped Meaning Anything
quote: the thing where you divide fractions
why: "the thing where" is the exact placeholder crutch phrase the rule names, standing in for the procedure instead of naming it
suggestion: They divide fractions by flipping the second one over.

rule_name: Hedge Where the Character Could Not Know, Cut Filler Everywhere Else
quote: She just doesn't know why it works
why: "just" softens an assertion the narrator can state plainly; not a hedge on an estimate Chloe couldn't be sure of
suggestion: She doesn't know why it works

rule_name: 2. Register: figurative language belongs in mouths
quote: which is a single syllable with his whole chest behind it
why: a newly built figurative image constructed by the narrator, not spoken or thought by a character, violating the rule that figurative language belongs in mouths
suggestion: Sam grunts, one syllable, loud.

quote: Kavi already knew it
why: asserts what Kavi knew internally before the scene, information the Chloe-limited narrator has no access to
suggestion: Kavi says he already knew it, out of a book

quote: Ruth has already gone past it and out the other side.
why: a newly built spatial metaphor for understanding, constructed by the narrator instead of placed in a character's mouth
suggestion: Ruth is already three questions past the board.

quote: without any comment about it
why: defines Mr. Baptiste's patience by the absence of a comment instead of stating what he does
suggestion: and redraws it exactly the same way

rule_name: Crutch Phrases That Have Stopped Meaning Anything
quote: for a while
why: "for a while" is used as a universal duration marker regardless of what kind of moment is being timed
suggestion: for the rest of the period

rule_name: Talking Heads, Anchor Dialogue in Physical Space
quote: Does it work with negative numbers?
why: opens a four-line exchange (through "Then it works.") with zero physical anchoring or attribution, leaving the reader without a room or a speaker
suggestion: A hand goes up near the back. "Does it work with negative numbers?"

rule_name: The Said-Bookism Overcorrection, Vary Attribution in Long Exchanges
quote: Then it works.
why: the fourth consecutive speaker turn in this exchange with no dialogue tag at all, leaving the reader to count lines to track who's speaking
suggestion: "Then it works," Mr. Baptiste says, capping the marker.

quote: What about zero.
why: repeats Ruth's line verbatim with no new information added by the repeat itself
suggestion: "Meaning?" Mr. Baptiste says.

rule_name: Crutch Phrases That Have Stopped Meaning Anything
quote: for a while
why: a second instance of "for a while" as a generic duration marker within a few lines of the first
suggestion: through the rest of the period

quote: There's a pool, and swimming is at four, and Chloe cannot swim.
why: three clauses of unequal weight (setting, schedule, personal deficiency) are chained flatly with "and...and" instead of being distinguished
suggestion: There's a pool. Swimming is at four. Chloe cannot swim.

quote: hates it more than Chloe does
why: states Ruth's comparative internal feeling as narrated fact rather than something Chloe can actually observe
suggestion: complains more than Chloe does

rule_name: Dialogue Tag Clutter, Let Action Beats Carry Tone
quote: Sam says, from the doorway, not stopping.
why: loads the tag with two circumstantial phrases explaining position and manner instead of giving the physical detail its own sentence
suggestion: Sam is already in the doorway, not stopping. "He went home."

quote: which is the part she can't get hold of
why: a trailing clause that tells the reader how to take the line instead of adding a new fact, the exact defect the trailing-clause rule targets
suggestion: Sam says it without any argument in it at all.

quote: without any argument in it at all
why: defines Sam's tone by the absence of argument rather than stating what his tone actually is
suggestion: Sam says it flat, like a fact.

quote: She can hear her own voice getting loud
why: routes the observation through the banned filter verb "hear" instead of rendering the voice directly
suggestion: Her own voice comes out loud, and she doesn't stop it.

quote: Chloe thinks about it on and off for the rest of the day and gets nowhere with it.
why: states that thinking occurred and failed instead of rendering the actual reasoning on the page
suggestion: Owen, then the bridge, then Owen again, and nowhere further than that.

quote: which is that Owen must not have liked the bridge
why: a trailing "which is" clause that glosses the previous statement instead of adding information, the construction Guide 2's checklist fails on sight
suggestion: She keeps landing in the same place: Owen must not have liked the bridge.

quote: There's a bed, and then there's a mattress.
why: the two halves mirror each other grammatically ("there's a X, and then there's a Y"), the symmetry construction the guide flags for rewrite
suggestion: The bed goes; the mattress stays, stripped bare.

rule_name: Paragraph Breaks, Keep One Beat in One Paragraph
quote: Sam looks at the table for a second.
why: splits one continuous beat, Sam pausing then answering, into two paragraphs (this line and the "No." that follows)
suggestion: Sam looks at the table for a second. "No."

rule_name: Crutch Phrases That Have Stopped Meaning Anything
quote: for a second
why: a universal duration marker used with no specific development of what kind of pause it is
suggestion: Sam looks at the table.

rule_name: Dialogue That States the Theme, Cut the Character's Gloss on Their Own Image
quote: "That's my whole thing," Chloe says.
why: this is the rule's own cited example verbatim: a character glossing the meaning of the image the scene already carried on its own
suggestion: Cut the line and end the beat on Sam's "But I'd say you were doing it on purpose."

quote: Chloe says
why: "Chloe says" is used as the dialogue tag three times within this one dinner-table passage (lines 86, 98, 101), the repeated-frame-verb pattern the checklist fails on sight
suggestion: Drop the tag here since the speaker is already clear: "Okay, but that's how it got that way. I'm talking about what it's doing now."

rule_name: Match Syntax to the Age, With the Ability Built In
quote: You can end up somewhere by accident and still be there.
why: this is the rule's own cited example verbatim: an abstract subordinate-clause construction too adult for a young child's dialogue
suggestion: You can end up somewhere by accident. You're still there though.

rule_name: Crutch Phrases That Have Stopped Meaning Anything
quote: doesn't use it for a second
why: another instance of the universal "for a second" duration marker with no specific development
suggestion: doesn't use it right away

quote: well past the point where he believes it
why: asserts Kavi's private belief state as narrated fact, information the Chloe-limited POV cannot access
suggestion: Kavi keeps arguing the moon is doing it deliberately, though his voice has gone flat.

quote: Chloe notices
why: "notices" is one of the exact filter verbs ("sees/hears/notices/knows") the rule names to cut
suggestion: Ten minutes into the walk back, it catches up with her.

rule_name: Crutch Phrases That Have Stopped Meaning Anything
quote: the part where she stopped and had a look at it and decided it was safe to say
why: "the part where" is one of the exact placeholder crutch phrases the rule names, standing in for behavior that should be shown
suggestion: looking for the moment she checked it before saying it

quote: Then she goes over the whole thing from the beginning
why: states that a review of her reasoning happened instead of rendering that review on the page
suggestion: Kavi, the moon, then her own mouth already moving before she'd looked at it.
